must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: Argo CD has had no health assessment for Application resources since 1.8, so platform-root's sync waves did not wait for strimzi-operator to become Healthy; the child Applications were created one right after the other and kafka-cluster and kafka-topics synced before the Strimzi CRDs existed.

Explains why they stay failed: automated sync does not retry a sync that failed against the same commit and parameters, so without a new commit (or a retry policy) the two apps stay in the failed state.

Restores the Application health check by adding resource.customizations.health.argoproj.io_Application (the Lua check from the Argo CD docs) to argocd-cm, so that each wave of platform-root waits until the child Application of the previous wave is Healthy.
Adds syncPolicy.retry (limit and backoff) to the child Applications, so a sync that fails because the CRDs are not there yet is retried until it succeeds.
Recovers staging now by triggering a manual sync of kafka-cluster and kafka-topics (argocd app sync, or Sync in the UI), since the CRDs now exist.

must_not.text: Recommends SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true on the Kafka apps as the fix on its own.
must_not.condition: only if presented as sufficient by itself; saying it does not help, or adding it next to a retry policy or a working wave order, does not count
must_not.near_miss: SkipDryRunOnMissingResource only skips the dry run; the Kafka resources still cannot be created while the Kafka CRD is missing.

reference:
Nothing held the Kafka apps back. Argo CD removed the health assessment of argoproj.io/Application resources in 1.8, so for platform-root a child Application has no health: wave 0 counted as done as soon as the strimzi-operator Application object existed, and waves 1 and 2 followed seconds later. Each child then synced on its own, and kafka-cluster and kafka-topics tried to create Kafka, KafkaNodePool and KafkaTopic resources before the Strimzi chart had installed the CRDs (the Kafka CRD was created 13 s after the failed sync started), hence 'the server could not find the requested resource'.
They stay failed because automated sync does not retry a sync that failed against the same commit and parameters, and you have no retry policy; only a new commit would trigger another attempt.
For the next environment:
1. Restore the Application health check: add resource.customizations.health.argoproj.io_Application (the Lua snippet from the Argo CD health docs) to argocd-cm. platform-root then waits in each wave until the child Application is Healthy.
2. Add syncPolicy.retry to the children (for example limit: 5, backoff duration 5s, factor 2, maxDuration 3m), so a sync that races a CRD is retried.
Recover staging now: the CRDs exist, so run argocd app sync kafka-cluster, then argocd app sync kafka-topics.
SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true would not help on its own: it skips only the dry run, and the apply still fails while the CRD is missing.
correct_alternative:
The ordering never existed: since Argo CD 1.8 an Application resource has no health status, so the parent's sync waves treat a child Application as done once it exists and do not wait for the Strimzi chart. kafka-cluster and kafka-topics synced in parallel with strimzi-operator, before the kafka.strimzi.io CRDs were installed, and failed. An automated sync that failed is not attempted again for the same commit and parameters, which is why they have sat there for three hours.
Make the children recover by themselves: give kafka-cluster and kafka-topics a syncPolicy.retry block, for example limit: 10 with backoff duration 10s, factor 2, maxDuration 3m. A sync that runs before the CRDs exist then fails, waits and succeeds once the chart has installed them.
For staging today, trigger a manual sync: argocd app sync kafka-cluster first, then argocd app sync kafka-topics.
SkipDryRunOnMissingResource alone would change nothing here, because the apply itself needs the CRD.
generic: The Kafka applications probably failed because of a dependency problem between your Argo CD applications. Check the Argo CD UI and the application controller logs for details, make sure the Strimzi operator pod is running and its CRDs are installed, and confirm that Argo CD has the RBAC permissions it needs on the destination cluster. Keeping your Git repository and Argo CD versions up to date also helps avoid such issues.
note: any_of m3/m4: either the restored Application health check or a retry policy makes the bootstrap reliable; the reference gives both, the alternative only the retry. SkipDryRunOnMissingResource is documented for CRDs that are not part of the sync but are created another way, for example by a controller (sync-options.md:83-97); it skips only the dry run, so it helps only if the CRD exists by the time the resource is applied. Here kafka-cluster applied its resources before the other Application had installed the CRD, so alone it changes nothing. The child Application objects do have a sync-wave annotation, which is valid but has no effect on ordering without the health check. Evidence: printer-column headers, field paths and the error message are exact; names, times and the jsonpath layout are invented.

must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: the group's committed offsets expired. offsets.retention.minutes (default 10080, 7 days) discards a group's committed offsets once the group has been empty that long, and with the monthly schedule the group was empty for four weeks.

Explains the empty file: with no committed offset the consumer applied auto.offset.reset, whose default is latest, so on 1 November it started at the end of each partition and skipped everything since 3 October.

Recovers October by resetting group billing-export with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --to-datetime set to the end of the last daily run (3 October, about 01:06 UTC) and then running the job once.
Prevents a repeat by raising offsets.retention.minutes on the brokers above the longest gap between two runs (it is a read-only broker setting, so it needs a broker restart).
Prevents a repeat by not depending on committed offsets between runs: the job stores where each export ended (offsets or the end timestamp) and seeks there at the next start.

Prevents a repeat by keeping the group from staying empty longer than offsets.retention.minutes (7 days by default), for example by running the job daily again and building the monthly file from the daily exports.

must_not.condition: only if recommended as the prevention or fix, alone or next to other measures, without deduplicating usage that was already exported; mentioning it to explain why it is unsafe here does not count, nor does earliest combined with deduplication of records already exported (for example by event id or by stored end offsets)
must_not.near_miss: earliest avoids the gap but, after the next expiry, re-reads all 45 days of usage-events, so already billed usage would be exported again.

must_not.text: Recommends resetting the group with --to-earliest (or deleting the group and re-reading from the start) for the recovery run.
must_not.condition: only if recommended for this recovery without filtering the output to records after the last daily run; describing it as the wrong option does not count, nor does re-reading from the earliest offset when the export then keeps only records produced after 3 October 01:06
must_not.near_miss: --to-datetime set to the end of the last good run re-reads only what was missed.

reference:
The group's committed offsets expired. offsets.retention.minutes (default 10080, 7 days) discards a group's committed offsets once the group has been empty that long. With the daily schedule the group was never empty for more than a day; after 3 October it was empty for four weeks, so around 10 October the offsets were gone. On 1 November the consumer found no committed offset and applied auto.offset.reset, default latest: it started at the end of every partition, exported only the 1,873 records that arrived during the run and committed those positions.
Recover October (the data is still there; with 45 days retention the oldest records you need are deleted from about 17 November, so do it this week):
1. Make sure no billing-export pod is running; the group must be inactive.
2. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server ... --group billing-export --topic usage-events --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-10-03T01:06:12.000 (no --execute, or --dry-run) and check the new offsets; then repeat with --execute. Without a zone suffix the time is UTC, like your log.
3. Run the job once; the file covers 3 October to now.
Prevent it: raise offsets.retention.minutes on the brokers above the longest gap between runs, for example 64800 (45 days); it is read-only, so it takes a rolling restart. Or make the job remember where each export ended and seek there itself.
Do not switch to auto.offset.reset=earliest: after the next expiry the job would re-read 45 days and bill weeks of usage twice.
correct_alternative:
Cause: Kafka expires a consumer group's committed offsets when the group has been empty for offsets.retention.minutes, 7 days by default. A monthly job leaves its group empty for about 30 days, so by 1 November nothing was committed, and the consumer fell back to auto.offset.reset, which defaults to latest: it jumped to the log end and found only the records produced during the run.
Fix October now: stop anything using the group, then use kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --group billing-export --topic usage-events --to-datetime 2026-10-03T01:06:12.000; look at the planned offsets first (default display or --dry-run), then rerun with --execute and start one job run. The 45-day retention still covers 3 October, but not for long.
Next month: stop relying on Kafka to keep the position for a month. Write the end offsets of each export to the job's own state (for example next to the CSV) and seek to them at start, falling back to an alert instead of a reset if they are missing. Do not use earliest, which would re-export old usage.
generic: This kind of problem usually comes from a consumer configuration issue. Check the consumer group with the Kafka tools, look at the job logs and the broker logs for errors, and make sure the job has the right permissions on the topic. For batch jobs, add monitoring on consumer lag and an alert when a run processes far fewer records than usual, so that missing data is detected earlier.
note: any_of m4a/m4b/m4c: all three prevent the next expiry (raise the retention, keep the position outside Kafka, or run often enough that the group is never empty for longer than the retention); the reference uses m4a, the alternative m4b; m4c was added by the second review. The Strimzi consumer page (con-consumer-config-properties.adoc:292-293) suggests earliest in general to avoid loss after offset expiry; for a billing export over a 45-day topic it duplicates usage, so n1 stands, and the second review scoped n1 so that earliest combined with deduplication does not count. The --to-datetime parsing (UTC without a zone suffix) is from raw_catalogue/apache-kafka-api/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/utils/Utils.java:1546-1548. Evidence: the job log is the application's own invented format; all values invented.

must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: spec.kafka.metadataVersion was never set, so Strimzi raised the metadata version to the 4.3 default by itself after the version change; the status shows kafkaMetadataVersion 4.3-IV0.

States that a downgrade to 4.2.x is not possible now: the cluster uses the latest metadata version of 4.3, which has metadata changes, and a downgrade is only possible when there are no metadata changes between the current and the target version.
Explains the CLI refusal: Argo CD cannot roll back an Application that has automated sync enabled.
For future upgrades, pins spec.kafka.metadataVersion in Git to the current value before changing spec.kafka.version, so the version change alone does not raise the metadata version.
Raises metadataVersion only later, in its own change, after the cluster has been verified on the new version, because raising it is what makes a downgrade impossible.

must_not.text: Recommends lowering the metadata version with kafka-features.sh downgrade (with or without --unsafe) so that the rollback becomes possible.
must_not.condition: only if recommended; mentioning the command to warn against it does not count
must_not.near_miss: kafka-features.sh downgrade --unsafe is documented by the tool itself as able to irreversibly destroy metadata, so it is not an option.

must_not.text: Recommends going ahead with the rollback to 4.2.2: turning off auto-sync and running argocd app rollback, reverting the Git commit, or first setting metadataVersion: 4.2-IV1 and then the version.
must_not.condition: only if recommended as the way to proceed for this cluster; describing the Strimzi downgrade procedure while saying it does not apply here does not count
must_not.near_miss: The documented downgrade (metadataVersion first, then version) works only while the cluster's metadata version is one the older Kafka supports, which is not the case here.

reference:
Stop: this cluster cannot go back to 4.2.
spec.kafka.metadataVersion was never set in Git, so once the brokers ran 4.3.1 Strimzi raised the metadata version to the 4.3 default by itself; that is the kafkaMetadataVersion: 4.3-IV0 in the status. The 4.3 metadata version has metadata changes, and Kafka allows a downgrade only when there are no metadata changes between the current and the target version, that is while the cluster still uses a metadata version that 4.2 supports. Strimzi's downgrade page says the same: a cluster already on the latest metadata version of its release cannot be downgraded. A git revert, an argocd app rollback with auto-sync off, or setting metadataVersion: 4.2-IV1 first will not get you to 4.2.2; do not try them on production.
The CLI refusal itself is expected: Argo CD does not roll back an Application with automated sync enabled.
Tonight: stay on 4.3.1 and work on the regression with the consumer team (client settings, or a later 4.3 patch release; Strimzi 1.3.1 also supports 4.3.2).
Next upgrade:
1. Pin spec.kafka.metadataVersion in Git to the current value (for example 4.2-IV1) before changing spec.kafka.version.
2. Change the version, let the rolling update finish, verify for some days.
3. Only then raise metadataVersion in a separate commit; that is the point of no return.
Do not use kafka-features.sh downgrade --unsafe; the tool warns it may irreversibly destroy metadata.
correct_alternative:
The status explains it: kafkaMetadataVersion is 4.3-IV0. Nobody pinned metadataVersion, so the operator moved it to the default for 4.3.1 right after the upgrade. Kafka's 4.3 upgrade notes say metadata downgrade is not supported for this version because it has metadata changes, and Strimzi's downgrade procedure adds that a cluster on the latest metadata version of its release cannot be downgraded. A rollback through Argo CD or Git would ask the operator for something Kafka refuses. The Argo CD refusal is separate and normal: rollback is not allowed while automated sync is on.
Plan instead: keep 4.3.1, find the cause of the consumer regression, and if it turns out to be a broker bug, move forward to a fixed 4.3.x rather than back.
In future upgrades keep spec.kafka.metadataVersion in Git at the old value through the version change, and bump it in its own commit only after the cluster has run well on the new version, because once it is raised there is no way back.
generic: Upgrades and rollbacks of Kafka on Kubernetes need care. Check the Kafka custom resource status and the Cluster Operator logs, compare the configuration in Git with what is running, and talk to the consumer team about the regression they see. Make sure you have a tested runbook and an agreed maintenance window before changing production, and keep Argo CD and Strimzi up to date.
note: No any_of: there is no correct path back to 4.2 here; the alternative is a reworded answer. Sources disagree: Strimzi's downgrade example (proc-downgrade-kafka-kraft.adoc) goes from 4.3.2 to 4.2.0 by setting metadataVersion: 4.2-IV1 first, while Kafka's 4.3 notes (upgrade.md:60) say metadata downgrade is not supported because 4.3-IV0 has metadata changes; the example can only hold for a cluster whose metadata version is still 4.2-IV1, which the same page's IMPORTANT note implies. con-upgrade-status.adoc renders kafkaMetadataVersion as 4.3 (attribute DefaultKafkaMetadataVersion), the upgrade example uses 4.3-IV0; the evidence uses 4.3-IV0. The exact text of Argo CD's rollback refusal is not in the sources, so it is described in prose. Evidence: field names and apiVersion exact; values invented.

must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: broker 6 was never cordoned, so between Monday's reassignment and Thursday's shutdown the controller still placed replicas of newly created partitions on it; audit-trail and invoices-v2 did not exist when Monday's plan was made.

Moves the broker-6 replicas of the 12 affected partitions to live brokers (1 to 5) with kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --execute, using a hand-written reassignment JSON or one made with --generate for just audit-trail and invoices-v2 and --broker-list 1,2,3,4,5.
After the reassignment has completed, unregisters broker 6 with kafka-cluster.sh unregister --id 6; it is still registered as a fenced broker.
Adds the missing first step to the runbook: cordon the broker before reassigning, with kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config cordoned.log.dirs="*" --entity-type brokers --entity-name <id>.
Notes that cordoning is new in Kafka 4.3 (KIP-1066), which is why a runbook written for earlier versions lacks it.

must_not.text: Recommends deleting and recreating audit-trail and invoices-v2.
must_not.condition: only if recommended as the fix or as the easier option; rejecting it does not count
must_not.near_miss: The two topics can stay; only their replicas on broker 6 have to move.

must_not.text: Claims that cordoning broker 6 now (setting cordoned.log.dirs) moves its existing replicas or clears the under-replicated partitions.
must_not.condition: whenever stated
must_not.near_miss: Cordoning only stops new assignments to the broker; existing replicas must be reassigned.

reference:
Broker 6 was never cordoned. Monday's plan covered only the topics that existed on Monday; until Thursday broker 6 was a normal, unfenced broker, so when audit-trail and invoices-v2 were created on Tuesday and Wednesday the controller placed replicas on it like on any other broker. Cordoning (cordoned.log.dirs) is what stops new partition assignments to a broker. When you stopped it, those 12 partitions lost one replica each; their leaders and the other two replicas are fine (ISR 2 of 3).
Now:
1. Do not recreate the topics, and you do not need the VM: the new replicas copy from the in-sync ones.
2. Write a reassignment JSON for the 12 partitions that replaces 6 with a broker from 1 to 5 not already in the list (or --generate for just these two topics with --broker-list 1,2,3,4,5), run kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --reassignment-json-file move-off-6.json --execute, then --verify with the same file until every partition is completed.
3. kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions should then print nothing.
4. Unregister the broker: kafka-cluster.sh unregister --bootstrap-server kafka-1.lan:9092 --id 6.
Runbook for Kafka 4.3 (cordoning is new in 4.3, KIP-1066):
1. Cordon: kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server ... --alter --add-config cordoned.log.dirs="*" --entity-type brokers --entity-name <id>.
2. Reassign all partitions off it; --execute, then --verify.
3. Check that no partition still lists the broker.
4. Shut it down and unregister it.
Cordoning alone moves nothing; the reassignment does.
correct_alternative:
What happened: nothing stopped the controller from using broker 6 after Monday. Since Kafka 4.3 (KIP-1066) the way to do that is to cordon the broker by setting cordoned.log.dirs, which blocks new partition assignments; you skipped it, so the topics created on Tuesday and Wednesday got replicas on 6, and those 12 partitions now run with two of three replicas.
Repair, no data lost and no VM needed: run kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --generate with a topics file holding only audit-trail and invoices-v2 and --broker-list 1,2,3,4,5, save the proposed assignment, apply it with --execute and repeat --verify with the same file until all partitions are completed. Then remove the dead registration with kafka-cluster.sh unregister --id 6. Recreating the topics would throw away their data for nothing.
Runbook order from now on: kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config cordoned.log.dirs="*" --entity-type brokers --entity-name <id>; reassign everything off the broker and verify; confirm with kafka-topics.sh --describe that the broker appears in no replica list; shut down; unregister.
generic: Under-replicated partitions mean that some replicas are not in sync with their leader. Check the broker logs and the network, look at disk and CPU usage on the brokers, and make sure all brokers are running. When a broker has been removed, update your monitoring, and make sure your decommissioning process is documented so it can be repeated reliably.
note: No any_of; the alternative differs in how the plan is made (--generate for the two topics instead of a hand-written JSON) and satisfies the same points. Kafka's decommissioning section (basic-kafka-operations.md:471-490) gives the cordon command but does not say what cordoning does; the statement that it prevents new partition assignments is in Strimzi's auto-rebalancing page (proc-automating-rebalances.adoc:20-21), hence the two pages. Evidence: the kafka-topics.sh line format (including Elr and LastKnownElr) is from TopicCommand.java:338-372 and the list-endpoints header and column widths from ClusterTool.java:191-199 (a null rack prints as null); host names, ids and partition placements are invented.

must.text: Says the templates produce a static quorum, not a dynamic one: a quorum is formatted as static when controller.quorum.voters is present at format time (a dynamic quorum requires it to be unset).
Replaces controller.quorum.voters with controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers listing the three controllers (host:port) in both the controller and the broker template.
Generates the cluster ID once for the whole cluster and formats every controller and broker with that same ID; provision.sh as written gives each host its own cluster ID.
Formats the three controllers with --initial-controllers listing all three as id@host:port:directory-id, with exactly the same value on every controller.

Formats one controller with --standalone and adds the other two afterwards with kafka-metadata-quorum.sh add-controller once they have caught up (the method the docs recommend for a new controller cluster).
Explains that a controller is added later (for the growth to five, or for a replacement VM) with kafka-metadata-quorum.sh add-controller, once the new controller has been started and has caught up.
Explains that a controller is removed from a dynamic quorum (the quorum is shrunk) with kafka-metadata-quorum.sh remove-controller.

must_not.condition: whenever recommended for this new cluster
must_not.near_miss: On an existing static cluster, controller.quorum.voters is replaced by controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers only after kraft.version has been upgraded to 1.

must_not.text: Says the format step can be dropped because Kafka formats empty storage and generates a cluster ID on first start.
must_not.condition: whenever stated
must_not.near_miss: Older Kafka versions formatted blank storage automatically; KRaft nodes must be formatted with kafka-storage.sh format.

must_not.text: Says the quorum as configured can later be grown or changed with kafka-metadata-quorum.sh add-controller or remove-controller, without first moving to a dynamic quorum.
must_not.condition: only if no move to a dynamic quorum (dynamic format, or kraft.version upgraded to 1) is part of the answer
must_not.near_miss: A static cluster can be moved to a dynamic quorum with kafka-features.sh upgrade --feature kraft.version=1 and a config change, and can then add controllers.

reference:
Three problems.
1. Static quorum. With controller.quorum.voters present when the storage is formatted, Kafka formats a static quorum. Only a dynamic quorum lets you add and remove controllers, which both requirements need. In both templates replace that line with
controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers=ctl-1.kafka.lan:9093,ctl-2.kafka.lan:9093,ctl-3.kafka.lan:9093
Every broker and controller sets it, and controller.quorum.voters must not be set.
2. Cluster ID. provision.sh calls random-uuid on every host, so all nine nodes get different cluster IDs. Generate the ID once in the pipeline and pass it to every host; the same ID must be used to format each server.
3. Format flags. Generate a directory ID per controller with random-uuid, then on each controller run
kafka-storage.sh format --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --initial-controllers "1@ctl-1.kafka.lan:9093:$DIR1,2@ctl-2.kafka.lan:9093:$DIR2,3@ctl-3.kafka.lan:9093:$DIR3" --config controller.properties
with exactly the same --initial-controllers value on all three. Format the brokers with
kafka-storage.sh format --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --config broker.properties --no-initial-controllers
Later, a replacement or extra controller is formatted with --no-initial-controllers, started, and once kafka-metadata-quorum.sh describe --replication shows it has caught up, added with kafka-metadata-quorum.sh add-controller; a controller is taken out of the quorum with remove-controller (the docs say to run it before the controller is shut down). Five controllers tolerate two failures instead of one.
correct_alternative:
The quorum would be static: controller.quorum.voters in the templates at format time gives a static voter set, and only a dynamic quorum supports adding and removing controllers. Use controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers with the three controller endpoints on all nine nodes instead, and drop controller.quorum.voters. The script also creates a new cluster ID on each host; create one ID up front and format every node with it.
Bootstrap the quorum the way the Kafka docs recommend for new clusters: format ctl-1 with kafka-storage.sh format --cluster-id <id> --standalone --config controller.properties and start it; format ctl-2, ctl-3 and all brokers with --no-initial-controllers. Start ctl-2, wait until kafka-metadata-quorum.sh describe --replication shows it has caught up, then run kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-controller ctl-1.kafka.lan:9093 --command-config controller.properties add-controller on ctl-2; repeat for ctl-3. Growing to five controllers later uses the same add-controller path.
generic: For a production KRaft cluster use dedicated controllers, an odd number of them, and keep their configuration consistent. Store the configuration in version control, use TLS on all listeners, monitor the controllers' metrics, and test controller failover before going live. Plan capacity for future growth and document the provisioning steps.
note: any_of m4a/m4b: both documented bootstrap methods for a dynamic quorum (--initial-controllers on all controllers, or --standalone plus add-controller). An answer that keeps the static templates and plans kafka-features.sh upgrade --feature kraft.version=1 (supported since 4.1, kraft.md:67-110) before the first controller change is workable but misses m2 and m4 as written; n3 is worded so it does not catch it. --no-initial-controllers is what the docs prescribe for brokers (kraft.md:145-151), but the tool enforces one of the three flags only on controllers when controller.quorum.voters is unset, and refuses --initial-controllers or --standalone while controller.quorum.voters is set (raw_catalogue/apache-kafka-tools/core/src/main/scala/kafka/tools/StorageTool.scala:146-168), so the broker flag is in the reference but not a must point. The near-miss names are controller.quorum.voters and controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers. The broker template needs no listener.security.protocol.map entry for CONTROLLER: KRaft assumes PLAINTEXT for the controller listener names when no mapping is given and no other protocol is in use (kafka_config.html:3359). Evidence: property names and kafka-storage.sh options exact; hosts, ids and paths invented. The second review split the old m5 into m5 (add-controller) and m6 (remove-controller); with the any_of group counted once the item has six units.

must.text: Says the namespaces: [kafka] selector must go (or andOperator: true be set), because the selectors of a window are ORed and it would also put kafka-topics-prod, which deploys into namespace kafka, under the Saturday-only window.
Says the window needs manualSync: true, because sync windows block manual syncs as well, so with only this allow window the on-call engineer could not sync outside Saturday 02:00 to 06:00.
Says syncOverrun does not give the on-call a manual sync: it only lets a sync that is already running continue after the window ends.
Adds timeZone: Europe/Berlin; without it the schedule is evaluated in UTC, so the window would open at 03:00 or 04:00 Berlin time.
Checks the result after the merge with argocd proj windows list kafka-prod (MANUALSYNC, TIMEZONE and USEANDOPERATOR columns) or argocd app get on the Applications (SyncWindow and Assigned Windows).

must_not.text: Says sync windows only restrict automated syncs, so manual syncs by the on-call engineer are always possible.
must_not.condition: whenever stated
must_not.near_miss: With manualSync: true on the window, manual syncs are allowed outside it.

must_not.text: Says the selectors of a window are combined with AND by default, so namespaces: [kafka] only narrows the window to the two named applications.
must_not.condition: whenever stated
must_not.near_miss: With andOperator: true the selectors are ANDed.

reference:
Four problems, one of them hidden by a comment.
1. Selectors are ORed. A window applies to an Application if any of applications, namespaces or clusters matches, so namespaces: [kafka] also catches kafka-topics-prod, which could then only sync on Saturday morning. Remove the namespaces entry (or set andOperator: true to AND the selectors).
2. The on-call cannot sync. Sync windows apply to manual syncs too: once an allow window matches an Application, syncs are only allowed while it is active. Set manualSync: true on the window to allow manual syncs outside it.
3. syncOverrun does not do what the comment says. It only lets a sync that is already running continue after the window ends; it is no manual override. It does no harm; keep it only if a sync that starts before 06:00 should be allowed to finish.
4. Time zone. Without timeZone the schedule is evaluated in UTC (the CLI default and the list output show UTC), so '0 2 * * 6' opens at 03:00 or 04:00 Berlin time. Add timeZone: Europe/Berlin.
Corrected window:
- kind: allow
  schedule: '0 2 * * 6'
  duration: 4h
  timeZone: Europe/Berlin
  applications: [kafka-cluster-prod, kafka-connect-prod]
  manualSync: true
After the merge, check argocd proj windows list kafka-prod (MANUALSYNC Enabled, TIMEZONE Europe/Berlin) and argocd app get kafka-cluster-prod and kafka-topics-prod, which show the SyncWindow state and the Assigned Windows.

must.text: Says the controller layout breaks requirement 2: KRaft needs a majority of the controllers alive, so losing the DC with two of the three controllers takes the cluster down; the controllers need a third location (for example one per site).
Says that with two rack values and replication factor 3 each partition spans only two racks, so two of its replicas sit in one DC.

Says acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 only guarantees the in-sync replicas: a write is acknowledged by the replicas currently in the ISR, which may be just the two in one DC, so an acknowledged write can be lost with that DC (requirement 1 fails).

Says that with only two data locations the two requirements conflict: no loss needs min.insync.replicas larger than the replicas in one DC (for example replication factor 4, two per DC, min.insync.replicas=3), and after losing a DC the two surviving replicas are below that, so acks=all writes fail with NotEnoughReplicas until someone intervenes.

Proposes a third site with brokers as well: broker.rack per site, replication factor 3 with one replica per site, min.insync.replicas=2 and one controller per site, so each acknowledged write is in two sites and the two remaining sites still meet the minimum.

Names the numbers still needed: latency and bandwidth to a third site, the cross-site replication traffic (60 MB/s for each replica outside the leader's site), and the producers' latency budget for acks=all across sites.

must_not.text: Says the proposal as written meets both requirements, or that acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 ensures every acknowledged write is in both DCs.
must_not.condition: whenever stated
must_not.near_miss: With all three replicas in the ISR, an acks=all write is on both DCs; the guarantee is lost when the ISR shrinks to the two replicas of one DC.

must_not.text: Recommends an even controller split over the two DCs (for example 2+2) to survive the loss of either DC.
must_not.condition: only if recommended as the fix for requirement 2
must_not.near_miss: Three controllers, one in each of three sites, keep a majority after any one site is lost.

must_not.text: Recommends enabling unclean.leader.election.enable so that writes continue after a DC loss.
must_not.condition: only if recommended; naming it to explain why it conflicts with requirement 1 does not count

reference:
No; it fails both requirements.
Controllers: KRaft needs a majority of the controllers alive. With two in DC-A and one in DC-B, losing DC-A leaves one of three: no quorum, so no leader elections or ISR changes, and writes stop. A 2+2 split would not help. You need a controller in a third location.
Data: with two rack values and replication factor 3, each partition spans min(2, 3) = 2 racks, so two replicas sit in one DC. acks=all means all replicas currently in the ISR, and min.insync.replicas=2 lets the ISR shrink to the two replicas of one DC, for example when the remote follower lags. Writes acknowledged then exist in one DC only and die with it.
With two data DCs the requirements conflict. No loss needs min.insync.replicas above the replicas in any one DC, for example replication factor 4 (2+2) with min.insync.replicas=3; after losing a DC only two replicas remain, below 3, so acks=all producers get NotEnoughReplicas until someone intervenes.
What meets both: a third site with brokers: broker.rack per site, replication factor 3 with one replica per site, min.insync.replicas=2, one controller per site. Every acknowledged write is in two sites, and after losing any site the other two keep the quorum and meet the minimum.
Unclean leader election is no way out; it can drop acknowledged data.
Still needed: latency and bandwidth to the third site, cross-site replication traffic (60 MB/s per replica outside the leader's site), and the producers' latency budget for acks=all.
correct_alternative: Requirement 2 already fails on the controllers: a KRaft quorum must keep a majority, and two of three controllers in DC-A means a DC-A outage leaves DC-B with one controller and no quorum. Requirement 1 fails on placement and min ISR: two rack values and three replicas put two replicas in one DC, and acks=all only waits for the replicas in the ISR, of which min.insync.replicas=2 lets two same-DC replicas be enough; those acknowledged writes die with that DC. With only two data DCs you have to choose: replication factor 4 with min.insync.replicas=3 gives no loss but stops acks=all writes (NotEnoughReplicas) after a DC failure; min ISR 2 keeps writing but can lose data. Both requirements together need three locations: one controller and a third of the brokers per site, broker.rack per site, replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2. Before sizing that, get the RTT and bandwidth to the third site, the cross-site traffic it adds (60 MB/s per remote replica) and the acceptable produce latency.
generic: A stretched cluster across two data centres can work when the latency is low. Use rack awareness so replicas are spread over both sites, use acks=all and a sensible min.insync.replicas, and monitor replication lag between the sites. Test failover regularly, make sure clients can reconnect to the surviving brokers, and keep MirrorMaker 2 as an option.
note: No any_of; the alternative is a reworded answer with the same conclusions. No page in the index treats a two-site stretched cluster; the facts (controller majority, racks spanned, ISR semantics of acks=all and min ISR) are indexed, but the trade-off between the two requirements (m4) and the three-site layout (m5) are inferences, hence not_indexed. Sources disagree within one page: datacenters.md:39 advises against a single cluster over a high-latency link and then says 'Kafka will remain available in all locations if the network between locations is unavailable', which reads like a missing 'not'. Today's MirrorMaker 2 setup is the documented pattern (datacenters.md:29), but asynchronous mirroring cannot meet requirement 1. Differs from p2-18 (MM2 DR design) and b1-10 (cross-zone cost): the subject here is the quorum and ISR guarantees of a two-site stretch.

must.text: Computes the needed concurrency: about 4,000/s x 0.6 s = 2,400 gateway calls in flight at peak (more at the 1.5 s tail), against 24 today.

Explains why more pods alone do not help in a consumer group: each partition is consumed by exactly one member of the group, so one-at-a-time processing is capped at the partition count, which is why the proposal needs 2,400 partitions.

Moves the unordered 98 % to a share group (production-ready since Kafka 4.2): share consumers cooperatively consume the partitions and can outnumber them, so concurrency scales without 2,400 partitions.

Keeps a consumer group but processes records concurrently inside each consumer (a bounded pool of in-flight calls per pod) and commits per partition only up to the highest offset below which every record is done.

Keeps per-user order for the security notifications on an ordered path, for example their own topic keyed by user id read by a consumer group, or strictly serial processing per user; they must not go through unordered parallel processing (a share group or a free worker pool).
Names the numbers still needed: the gateway's rate or concurrency limit, the acceptable notification delay at peak, and the failure and retry rate.

must_not.text: Puts the security notifications into the share group (or an unordered worker pool) and says per-user order is kept because the records are keyed by user id.
must_not.condition: whenever proposed
must_not.near_miss: In a consumer group, records with the same key stay in order because each partition has one consumer.

must_not.text: Says a share group delivers each record exactly once, so no duplicate notifications can occur.
must_not.condition: whenever stated
must_not.near_miss: A record that is released, or whose acquisition lock expires, is delivered again, so duplicates are possible.

reference:
The proposal follows from consumer-group mechanics: each partition is read by exactly one member of the group, so with one call at a time you get at most one call per partition in flight. At 4,000/s x 0.6 s you need about 2,400 calls in flight (more on the 1.5 s tail), hence 2,400 partitions. It would work, but it ties throughput to the partition count and buys many partitions and pods for what is mostly waiting on I/O.
Split by requirement:
1. Bulk (98 %): consume with a share group (production-ready since Kafka 4.2). Share consumers cooperatively consume the partitions and can outnumber them, so you scale consumers without repartitioning; 24 partitions can stay. Use explicit acknowledgement (share.acknowledgement.mode=explicit): ACCEPT after a successful send, RELEASE on a transient gateway error for another attempt, REJECT when you would park it. Delivery attempts are counted and capped by share.delivery.count.limit (default 5), which replaces most of the retry code. Redelivery can happen, so make sends idempotent.
2. Security (2 %): keep them ordered. Produce them to their own topic keyed by user id and consume it with a consumer group, one record at a time per partition. About 80/s x 0.6 s = 48 calls in flight, so give that topic at least about 50 partitions.
Still needed: the gateway's rate or concurrency limit (2,400 parallel calls may exceed it), the acceptable delay at peak, and the failure and retry rate.
correct_alternative: A consumer group gives each partition to exactly one member, so processing one record at a time caps you at 24 calls in flight, while 4,000/s at 0.6 s needs about 2,400. Instead of 2,400 partitions, keep consumer groups and stop processing one record at a time: each pod runs a bounded pool of asynchronous gateway calls, for example up to 100 in flight, so 24 pods cover the load. Commit per partition only up to the highest offset below which every record has finished, never past a gap, so a crash replays unfinished work instead of dropping it. Records of the same user must not run in parallel: give each user key its own serial lane inside the pod, which keeps the security notifications in order. Failures go to a retry topic and then the parking topic so they do not block the lane. Before sizing, find out the gateway's concurrency limit, the acceptable delay at peak and the retry rate.
generic: To handle more load, scale out the consumers and spread the work over more partitions. Use asynchronous processing where possible, monitor consumer lag and set alerts on it, make sure failed notifications are retried and dead-lettered, and test the new design under peak load before going live.
note: any_of m3a/m3b: a share group for the unordered bulk, or in-process concurrency in a consumer group with gap-free commits; the reference takes the first, the alternative the second, and m4 is worded for both. The acknowledgement types (AcknowledgeType ACCEPT, RELEASE, REJECT) are in the pinned client source raw_catalogue/apache-kafka-api/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer/AcknowledgeType.java:27-36; share.acknowledgement.mode and share.delivery.count.limit are in the 4.3 config pages. Sources disagree on the per-partition lock limit's name: design.md:277 calls it the broker property group.share.partition.max.record.locks, the 4.3 notes (upgrade.md) add a group config share.partition.max.record.locks; the item does not depend on it. Overlap check: b1-01 is about share-group lock expiry with implicit acknowledgement; here lock duration plays no part (each call is far below 30 s) and the subject is the choice between share and consumer groups.

reference:
Enabling the User Operator changed who owns the users. It manages the SCRAM-SHA credentials, ACLs and quotas of every user in the cluster that its ignore pattern does not exclude, and users without a KafkaUser resource are removed. At 16:45 it therefore deleted the credentials and ACLs of etl-loader, bi-reader and ci-admin, which only the CI job knew about. Your output shows it: SCRAM credentials exist only for the four KafkaUsers and no ACLs are left for the legacy principals. The listeners did not change.
Fix it one of two ways:
1. Manage them with the User Operator (preferred): create KafkaUsers etl-loader, bi-reader and ci-admin with authentication type scram-sha-512 and their ACLs under authorization type simple. To keep the passwords the jobs use, store each one in a Secret and reference it with spec.authentication.password.valueFrom.secretKeyRef; otherwise the operator generates a new password.
2. Or keep them outside: set STRIMZI_IGNORED_USERS_PATTERN, for example ^(etl-loader|bi-reader|ci-admin)$, in spec.entityOperator.template.userOperatorContainer.env of the Kafka resource, wait for the Entity Operator to restart, then re-create the credentials with kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config 'SCRAM-SHA-512=[password=<existing>]' --entity-type users --entity-name <user> and the ACLs with kafka-acls.sh.
Do not simply re-run the CI job before one of these, or the operator removes the users again. Then check with kafka-configs.sh --describe --entity-type users that the three users have SCRAM-SHA-512 credentials, and rerun the jobs. Do not open access with allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found or superUsers.
correct_alternative: The User Operator was switched on without being told which users to leave alone. It treats every user it does not ignore as its own, so the SCRAM credentials and ACLs of etl-loader, bi-reader and ci-admin, which have no KafkaUser, were deleted; describe shows credentials only for the four KafkaUsers and the ACL listings are empty. Since the CI job should keep owning these accounts, exclude them: add STRIMZI_IGNORED_USERS_PATTERN with the value ^(etl-loader|bi-reader|ci-admin)$ under spec.entityOperator.template.userOperatorContainer.env and let the Entity Operator roll. Then, as ops-admin, restore each user with kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config 'SCRAM-SHA-512=[password=<the job's current password>]' --entity-type users --entity-name <user>, and re-apply their ACLs with kafka-acls.sh (or re-run the CI job, which is now safe). Confirm with kafka-configs.sh --describe --entity-type users that all three have SCRAM-SHA-512 credentials again before restarting the jobs. Moving them to KafkaUsers later would end the split ownership.
generic: SCRAM authentication failures usually mean the username or password is wrong or the mechanism does not match. Check the client configuration of the jobs, make sure they use SASL_SSL with SCRAM-SHA-512 and the right truststore, and look at the broker logs for authentication errors. Compare the job configuration with a service that still works, and rotate the passwords if you suspect they leaked.
note: m1 rests on two pages: the ignore page says what the User Operator stops managing for an excluded user, and the recovery page warns that, with the User Operator enabled, users without a KafkaUser are deleted (second review: the chunks hold the fact). The ignore page names the path as .spec.teplate.entityOperator.userOperatorContainer.env (typo, wrong order); its example and the CRD reference (appendix_crds.adoc:1387) give spec.entityOperator.template.userOperatorContainer.env. Second review: the fix is three steps, each an any_of group with the KafkaUser route and the ignore-pattern route as members: ownership [m2a, m2b], existing passwords [m3, m6], ACLs [m5, m7]; an answer that mixes the routes can collect members it does not deserve as a whole, which a reader would see. The CI job can only re-create ACLs after ci-admin is restored, since its own credentials were deleted too. The correct alternative takes m2b, m6 and m7 and re-runs the CI job only after the ignore pattern, so n3 does not apply.
