The task was restarted at about 01:58, 02:00, 02:06, 02:18, 02:38 and 03:08 (count 6), all while the database was down, so the next attempt was due 42 minutes after 03:08, about 03:50. That restart brought it back; nothing retried between 03:15 and 03:50.
Second, strimzi.io/restart="true" restarts only the connector instance. Its options includeTasks and onlyFailed both default to false, so the connector (already RUNNING) was restarted, task 0 was left FAILED, and the annotation was removed as soon as Connect accepted the request.
What the on-call should do once the database is back: restart the task itself with kubectl annotate kafkaconnector orders-pg-sink -n data strimzi.io/restart-task="0" (or strimzi.io/restart="includeTasks,onlyFailed"), wait for the next reconciliation (two minutes by default) and check status.connectorStatus.tasks. No need to touch the worker pods or the other 12 connectors.
maxRestarts: 3 would not make retries faster. It only caps the number of automatic restarts, which is unlimited by default; during a long outage the operator would stop after the third attempt and someone would have to restart the connector by hand. Also, the counter resets only after the connector has run longer than the next interval; after seven restarts that is 56 minutes, so a new failure within that time continues with long gaps. Put the task restart into the database maintenance runbook.
correct_alternative: The task stayed FAILED because of how both mechanisms work. Automatic restarts use an increasing back-off of n*n+n minutes after n restarts, at most 60. Six restarts were spent during the outage, the last at 03:08, so the seventh came 42 minutes later, at 03:50, exactly when it recovered. The manual annotation strimzi.io/restart="true" did fire, but by default it restarts only the connector, not its tasks (includeTasks=false, onlyFailed=false). Next time, once the database is reachable, annotate with strimzi.io/restart="includeTasks,onlyFailed", which restarts the connector and only its FAILED task, and check the task state after the next reconciliation. maxRestarts is only an upper limit on automatic attempts; it does not shorten the intervals, and after the limit the connector stays failed until someone restarts it. The counter returns to 0 only when the connector has run longer than the next interval, so a second outage soon after starts again with long gaps.
generic: Connector tasks can fail when a downstream database is unavailable. After an outage, check the connector status and the worker logs, make sure the database is reachable from the Connect pods, and restart the connector if it does not recover. Consider tuning the connector's own retry settings for database errors, and alert on FAILED tasks so the on-call notices sooner.
note: The restart times are computed from the documented formula, reading the listed 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 42, 56 minutes as gaps between consecutive restarts; the page's wording could also be read as minutes after the first failure, which does not fit the recorded lastRestartTimestamp. m3c (REST API) is correct but needs access to the REST service, which Strimzi restricts by network policy; from inside a Connect pod it works. The correct alternative takes m3b. The generic answer's 'restart the connector' is the advice that failed here and earns no point.

must.text: Says the plan is not safe: the data is still on the Released PVs (reclaim policy Retain), but a Released PV is not available for another claim, so recreating the cluster before the old PVs are bound again would give the brokers and controllers new, empty volumes.

Turns off automated sync of kafka-core before the namespace exists again (for example spec.syncPolicy.automated.enabled: false, or removing the automated block), because with automated sync and selfHeal Argo CD would apply everything from Git as soon as the namespace is back.
Recreates each PVC with its original name (data-0-core-broker-0 to data-0-core-controller-5), size and storage class, with spec.volumeName set to the PV shown for it in the CLAIM column.
Removes the claimRef from each of the six PVs so that they can bind to the new PVCs.
Recreates the KafkaUser Secrets from the copies, with exactly the same names, labels and fields, before the KafkaUsers are applied; otherwise the User Operator generates new passwords.

Makes sure the recreated Kafka resource carries the original cluster ID before the operator reconciles it: applies it with strimzi.io/pause-reconciliation="true", sets .status.clusterId (read from meta.properties on a recovered volume) with kubectl edit kafka core --subresource status, then unpauses.

must_not.text: Recommends recreating the namespace while automated sync is still on, or syncing kafka-core (Kafka and the KafkaNodePools) before the PVCs are recreated and bound to the old PVs.
must_not.condition: only if this order is recommended; recreating the namespace after automated sync is off and then creating the PVCs does not count
must_not.near_miss: Recreate the namespace with automated sync turned off, then create the PVCs with volumeName before anything from Git is applied.

must_not.text: Says the old PVs bind again by themselves when PVCs with the same names are created, with no volumeName and no change to claimRef.
must_not.condition: only if stated as sufficient; describing volumeName together with removing claimRef does not count
must_not.near_miss: A PVC that names the PV in spec.volumeName binds to it once the PV's claimRef has been removed.

reference:
Not safe. The data survived: the PVs have reclaim policy Retain and are Released, but a Released PV is not available for another claim. If the namespace comes back while kafka-core auto-syncs (selfHeal and unlimited retry), Argo CD applies Kafka and the node pools at once, the operator creates new PVCs, and they get new, empty volumes.
Order:
1. Turn off auto-sync (spec.syncPolicy.automated.enabled: false on kafka-core), then terminate the still-retrying sync (argocd app terminate-op kafka-core), which auto-sync off does not stop.
2. terraform apply to recreate the namespace.
3. Recreate the six PVCs with their old names (data-0-core-broker-0 ... data-0-core-controller-5), same size, storageClassName ssd-retain and spec.volumeName set to the PV from the CLAIM column.
4. Delete spec.claimRef from each PV; check the PVCs become Bound.
5. Recreate the KafkaUser Secrets from the apps' copies with the same names, labels and keys, before any KafkaUser exists, or the User Operator generates new passwords.
6. Apply the KafkaTopics unchanged from Git, then the KafkaUsers.
7. Add strimzi.io/pause-reconciliation: "true" to Kafka core in Git and apply Kafka and both node pools.
8. Read cluster.id from meta.properties on data-0-core-broker-0 (temporary pod), set .status.clusterId with kubectl edit kafka core -n kafka --subresource status, then unpause.
9. Check that the nodes keep ids 0-2 and 3-5 (pin them with strimzi.io/next-node-ids if needed), watch the KafkaTopics become Ready, then remove the annotation in Git and turn auto-sync back on.
The CA Secrets were deleted too: expect new CAs, so TLS clients need the new core-cluster-ca-cert.
correct_alternative: Do not let Argo CD rebuild it yet. Your PVs kept the data (Retain), but they are Released, which means Kubernetes will not hand them to a new claim; a full sync would make Strimzi create fresh PVCs on fresh disks and start an empty cluster with a new ID. First remove the automated block from kafka-core's syncPolicy and terminate the sync that is still retrying (Sync status, then Terminate), because that operation keeps its own retries; then create the namespace. Create PVCs data-0-core-broker-0/1/2 and data-0-core-controller-3/4/5 by hand, each with volumeName pointing at its old PV, and clear claimRef on those PVs until all six are Bound. Restore the user Secrets from the application namespaces (same name, labels, keys) before any KafkaUser is created. Apply topics and users, then kubectl apply the Kafka resource with strimzi.io/pause-reconciliation="true" plus the two node pools. Take cluster.id from meta.properties on one volume, write it into status.clusterId through the status subresource, unpause, and re-enable automated sync once everything is Ready.
generic: Deleting a namespace removes all resources in it. Check whether you have backups of the cluster and its data, and restore from them if possible. Since everything is in Git, Argo CD can recreate the resources; after the sync, verify that the Kafka cluster becomes Ready, that topics and users exist, and that clients can connect. To prevent this in the future, protect production namespaces from deletion.
note: No any_of group; the correct alternative is a re-worded answer that turns off auto-sync by removing spec.syncPolicy.automated (auto_sync.md:34) and applies the paused Kafka resource with kubectl. Not covered by the procedure page: KafkaNodePools (it speaks of the Kafka resource only), node-ID assignment of recreated pools, and the deleted cluster and clients CA Secrets; the reference mentions them as cautions, not as points. The procedure page also tells you to deploy the Cluster Operator into the namespace; here it runs elsewhere, so that step does not apply. Second review: the sync that is retrying when automated sync is turned off keeps retrying, because the operation carries its own retry strategy (Application CRD operation.retry); the reference and the alternative terminate it. It is not a point: the 3-to-6 cap is reached, and the need for it rests on the CRD, which is outside the index (faq.md:152-156 in the index only shows how to terminate a sync).

must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: the custom certificate's SANs cover only the bootstrap service, but a listener certificate must name every broker as well; after bootstrapping, clients connect to each broker by its advertised hostname (core-broker-N.core-kafka-brokers.kafka.svc), which is not in the certificate, so hostname verification fails on every broker connection while the bootstrap connection passes.

Has the certificate reissued with SANs for every broker as well as the bootstrap service, for example *.core-kafka-brokers and *.core-kafka-brokers.kafka.svc plus core-kafka-bootstrap and core-kafka-bootstrap.kafka.svc (or each broker hostname listed), and writes it to the same Secret.

Notes that broker hostnames are advertised without the .cluster.local suffix by default (useServiceDnsDomain: false), so the SANs must contain the .svc form; the .svc.cluster.local form is only used with useServiceDnsDomain: true.
Says that updating the certificate in the Secret the listener already uses starts a rolling update of the brokers by itself; no change to the Kafka resource is needed.

Warns that maintenanceTimeWindows do not apply to custom listener certificates: every 30-day renewal written to the Secret rolls the brokers immediately, outside the Sunday window, so the renewal sync should be scheduled inside the window if that matters.

must_not.text: Recommends disabling hostname verification on the clients (ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm set to an empty string) as the fix or as a lasting workaround for this internal listener.
must_not.condition: only if recommended for this listener; explaining that Strimzi documents it for nodeport listeners, where it cannot put node addresses into the certificate, does not count
must_not.near_miss: The Strimzi page that says to disable hostname verification is about nodeport listeners; here the fix is to put the broker names into the certificate.

must_not.text: Says the clients must trust the Strimzi cluster CA (core-cluster-ca-cert) to fix this handshake error.
must_not.condition: only if offered as the fix for this error; saying that other listeners still use the cluster CA does not count
must_not.near_miss: Clients must trust the CA that signed the listener certificate, here the internal PKI root they already have.

reference:
The certificate names only the bootstrap service. A client's first connection goes to core-kafka-bootstrap.kafka.svc, which matches, and returns the metadata; after that the client connects to each broker by its advertised name, core-broker-N.core-kafka-brokers.kafka.svc, which is not in the SANs, so hostname verification fails on every broker connection. For a custom listener certificate the SANs must cover all brokers and the bootstrap service.
Fix: have the PKI reissue the certificate with
- *.core-kafka-brokers and *.core-kafka-brokers.kafka.svc (or each core-broker-0/1/2 name in both forms),
- core-kafka-bootstrap and core-kafka-bootstrap.kafka.svc,
and write it into the same Secret core-tls-listener. Brokers are advertised without .cluster.local unless useServiceDnsDomain: true, so the .svc form is the one that must be there. Updating the certificate in a Secret a listener already uses starts a rolling update by itself; the Kafka resource needs no change. Check afterwards with openssl x509 -ext subjectAltName and a test producer.
Do not set ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm= : the Strimzi page that says so is about nodeport listeners, where Strimzi cannot know the node addresses; here it would only switch off server authentication.
About the 30-day renewals: Strimzi does not manage or renew this certificate, and maintenanceTimeWindows do not apply to custom listener certificates. Every renewal your sync job writes rolls all brokers immediately, so let the job write the Secret only inside your Sunday 00:00-01:59 UTC window, which the PKI renewal margin must allow.
correct_alternative: Your listener certificate is valid for the bootstrap name and nothing else. Kafka clients use the bootstrap address only to fetch metadata; then they open connections to each broker under the address that broker advertises, here core-broker-0/1/2.core-kafka-brokers.kafka.svc (no .cluster.local, because useServiceDnsDomain defaults to false). Those names are missing from the SANs, so the Java client rejects them. Request a new certificate that lists core-broker-0.core-kafka-brokers.kafka.svc, core-broker-1.core-kafka-brokers.kafka.svc and core-broker-2.core-kafka-brokers.kafka.svc, their short forms without .kafka.svc, and core-kafka-bootstrap plus core-kafka-bootstrap.kafka.svc; add names for new broker ids before you scale. Replace tls.crt and tls.key in core-tls-listener; the operator sees the Secret change and rolls the brokers. Keep hostname verification on. Rolls caused by this externally managed certificate ignore maintenanceTimeWindows, so with 30-day renewals have the sync job update the Secret only during the Sunday window.
generic: SSL handshake failures usually come from certificate problems. Check that the certificate is valid and not expired, that the client truststore contains the right CA, and that the TLS versions and cipher suites on client and broker match. Look at the broker logs during the handshake, and renew certificates well before they expire.
note: No any_of group; the correct alternative is a re-worded answer that lists the broker names instead of wildcards (both meet m2). The non-wildcard example on the SAN page uses the old pod names <cluster>-kafka-0; with node pools the pods are <cluster>-<pool>-<id>, so the wildcards are the safer reading. The DNS-name form of the JDK exception is my wording by analogy with the IP-address form on con-hostname-verification-node-ports.adoc:20; the openssl output layout is from memory.

must.text: Requires a unique groupId and unique names for the three storage topics (for example analytics-connect and analytics-connect-configs, -offsets, -status); with the copied values both deployments form one logical Connect cluster that shares the internal topics.

Grants the analytics Connect user ACLs under the new names: Describe, Read and Write (and Create unless the topics exist) on its own three storage topics and Read on its own group; etl-connect's ACLs name etl-connect's group and topics, so the 'no new ACLs' argument does not hold.
Recommends creating the three storage topics up front (for example as KafkaTopic resources): the config topic with a single partition, and all three replicated and compacted.

must_not.text: Approves applying the manifest with groupId etl-connect and the etl-connect-* storage topics unchanged.
must_not.condition: only if approved as is or called acceptable; quoting the values that must change does not count
must_not.near_miss: Each Connect cluster on the same Kafka cluster needs its own groupId and its own config, offset and status topics.

must_not.text: Recommends broad access instead of specific ACLs: making the Connect user a super user, ACLs on all topics or groups ('*'), or allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true.
must_not.condition: only if recommended; prefixed ACLs limited to the analytics-connect name prefix do not count
must_not.near_miss: Prefixed ACLs on the prefix analytics-connect cover exactly its own storage topics and group and are fine.

reference:
Do not apply it as is.
1. groupId and storage topics: every Kafka Connect instance on the same Kafka cluster needs its own groupId and its own config, offset and status topics. With groupId etl-connect and the etl-connect-* topics, the analytics workers would join etl-connect's group and share its internal state (connector configurations, offsets, status): one logical cluster, with unexpected errors for both teams. Use for example groupId analytics-connect and the topics analytics-connect-configs, analytics-connect-offsets and analytics-connect-status.
2. ACLs: the argument is backwards. Reusing the user avoids new ACLs only while group and topics are shared, which is exactly what must not happen. With unique names the Connect user needs Describe, Read and Write on the three new storage topics (Create too if Connect should create them) and Read on group analytics-connect, using the configured names, plus Read on clicks and sessions and on the groups its sink connectors use. Create a dedicated KafkaUser analytics-connect (scram-sha-512) with exactly these ACLs and let the sync job copy its Secret; sharing etl-connect's credentials also gives each team the other's rights.
3. Storage topics: create them up front as KafkaTopics in namespace kafka: the config topic with one partition, all three compacted and with replication factor 3. Then the Create ACL is not needed.
tls.trustedCertificates and the scram-sha-512 authentication block stay as they are, pointing at the new user and its Secret. Apply once the KafkaUser is Ready.
correct_alternative: Two blockers. The manifest reuses etl-connect's groupId and its configs, offsets and status topics; two Connect deployments with the same group ID and internal topics become a single logical cluster and share state, so rename them, for example to analytics-connect and analytics-connect-configs/-offsets/-status. Once renamed, the claim that the shared user needs no new ACLs is the wrong way round: etl-connect's ACLs name etl-connect's group and topics, not the new ones. Give analytics-connect its own KafkaUser with prefixed ACLs on the prefix analytics-connect (topics: Describe, Read, Write, Create; group: Read), plus read access to clicks and sessions for the connectors. Better still, create the internal topics beforehand: configs with one partition, and all three compacted and replicated three times; Create is then unnecessary. Keep the TLS trust and SCRAM settings, change username and passwordSecret to the new user.
generic: Reusing configuration between Kafka Connect clusters can save time, but review it carefully. Make sure the bootstrap address, TLS and authentication settings are right for the target cluster, that replication factors fit the cluster size, and that the Connect cluster has enough replicas and resources. Test the connectors in a non-production environment before going live.
note: Three units: a configuration review with two blockers and one recommendation; it should be answerable from the two Connect pages (one or two pages). No any_of group; the correct alternative is a re-worded answer that uses prefixed ACLs, the near miss of n2. Not a point: what each operator does with the other team's connectors when both share a group (the multiple-instances page only says 'unexpected errors').

must.text: Adds generateCertificateAuthority: false to clusterCa and to clientsCa; it is required (must be false) when type is cert-manager.

Changes the KafkaUser authentication type from tls to tls-external: with cert-manager the operator does not issue client certificates (the clientsCa issuerRef is not used for that); they are issued by your own cert-manager Certificate.
Sets the Certificate's commonName to the KafkaUser name, orders-api, because Kafka uses the CN of the client certificate as the principal for authentication and authorization.
Reorders ca.crt in stage-ca-chain: the intermediate CA first and the root CA last.
Corrects the assumption about renewals: maintenance time windows do not apply to certificates issued by cert-manager, so its renewals roll the pods whenever cert-manager renews.
Flags that the cert-manager integration is Early Access in Strimzi 1.3 and not recommended for production, so the production date needs an explicit decision.

must_not.text: Recommends or accepts a public CA (for example the ACME ClusterIssuer) as the issuer behind clusterCa.
must_not.condition: only if recommended or accepted for the cert-manager issuer of the cluster CA; a publicly signed certificate on a listener through brokerCertChainAndKey does not count
must_not.near_miss: A publicly signed certificate can be used for a listener through brokerCertChainAndKey, but the issuer behind clusterCa must be a private CA because the certificates carry internal service names.

reference:
Findings:
1. clusterCa and clientsCa: add generateCertificateAuthority: false to both. It is required (must be false) with type: cert-manager.
2. KafkaUser orders-api: use authentication type tls-external, not tls. With cert-manager the operator does not issue client certificates (clientsCa.certManager.issuerRef is only required by the schema); you issue them with your own Certificate, as the PR does.
3. Certificate orders-api: commonName must be orders-api, the KafkaUser name. Kafka takes the CN as the principal, so with orders-api.kafka-stage.svc the ACLs would never match. Its issuer kafka-int is backed by the same CA as clientsCa.caCertRef, as required.
4. stage-ca-chain: intermediate first, root last; the CI cat order is reversed.
5. Renewals: maintenance time windows do not apply to certificates issued by cert-manager. cert-manager renews on its own schedule and the operator then rolls the pods at once, so expect rolls outside Sunday 00:00-01:59.
6. Production: the cert-manager integration is Early Access in Strimzi 1.3 and not recommended for production; production in two weeks needs an explicit decision.
Also expect on this existing cluster a multiphase rolling restart, and the operator deletes stage-cluster-ca and stage-clients-ca (the old CA keys); keep a copy if you want a way back.
The ACME issuer is no option for clusterCa: the certificates carry internal Kubernetes names that public CAs cannot sign, so the CA behind the issuer must be private.
correct_alternative: Not ready to merge. The Kafka resource lacks generateCertificateAuthority: false under clusterCa and clientsCa; the cert-manager type requires it. The user side is mixed up: when cert-manager issues the certificates, client certificates are your job, so orders-api must be a tls-external KafkaUser (no credentials generated by the operator), and the Certificate that issues it must carry commonName orders-api, the KafkaUser name, which Kafka will use as the principal for the ACLs; orders-api.kafka-stage.svc would not match. The trust bundle is in the wrong order: ca.crt must list the intermediate before the root. Your maintenance window will not hold either: maintenance time windows are not applied to cert-manager-issued certificates, so renewal rolls happen whenever cert-manager renews. Finally, cert-manager support arrived in Strimzi 1.3 as Early Access and is not recommended for production, so production in two weeks is a risk to decide on. Public ACME certificates cannot cover the internal service names, so keep the private intermediate.
generic: Using cert-manager for Kafka certificates is a good idea for automation. Make sure cert-manager is healthy, that the issuer is Ready, and that certificates are renewed well before they expire. Test the change in staging first, monitor the rolling restarts, and confirm that clients can still connect with their new certificates. Document the rollback procedure.
note: No any_of group; the correct alternative is a re-worded answer. The CRD reference and the procedure agree on the field names (appendix_crds.adoc:1505-1580). The public-CA question in the prompt is covered by the must-not only; an answer may leave it out without losing a point.

must.text: Attaches a source partition and a source offset to every SourceRecord, for example sourcePartition {"region": "eu"} and sourceOffset {"cursor": ...}, so that Connect commits the cursor together with the records.
On start, reads the last committed cursor with context.offsetStorageReader().offset(<partition map>) and starts from the beginning only when it returns null.

Adds the ServiceLoader manifest META-INF/services/org.apache.kafka.connect.source.SourceConnector containing the connector's fully qualified class name, because with plugin.discovery=service_load a plugin without a manifest is not found.
Implements taskConfigs(maxTasks) so that it returns one task configuration per region (eu, us), each task owning one source partition.
When the API returns no items, poll() waits (sleeps or blocks, which is allowed because each task has its own thread) and returns no records, instead of calling the API in a tight loop.

Makes stop() safe to call from a thread other than the one running poll() (for example a synchronized stop(), or a thread-safe stop flag that poll() checks), because each task polls in its own thread and may block there.

must_not.text: Keeps the cursor in a local file, in an external store, or through commit()/commitRecord() as the way to resume, instead of source offsets.
must_not.condition: only if this replaces source offsets as the resume mechanism; using commit() or commitRecord() only to acknowledge records in the source system does not count
must_not.near_miss: commit() and commitRecord() exist for acknowledging in the source system; Connect records the source offsets itself.

must_not.text: Recommends setting plugin.path (or another plugin.path value) in the KafkaConnect spec.config to make the plugin visible.
must_not.condition: only if recommended; noting that Strimzi manages the plugin path does not count
must_not.near_miss: Strimzi sets the plugin path itself; add the plugin through spec.build or the image, and give it a ServiceLoader manifest.

generic: To write a Kafka Connect source connector, extend the connector and task base classes, implement start, stop and poll, and package the connector as a JAR. Handle errors from the REST API with retries, log useful information, and make the connector configurable. Deploy the JAR to your Connect workers and create the connector through the REST API or a KafkaConnector resource.
note: No any_of group; the correct alternative is a different correct implementation (AtomicBoolean instead of synchronized stop, empty list instead of null). Not a point but worth a reader's eye: if every record of a page carries next_cursor and the worker dies after only some of them were written, the committed offset can skip the rest of the page; both answers give the earlier cursor to all records but the last (second review: the alternative was changed to do so). version() is required by the Connect API but is not in the pinned docs, so neither answer shows it. An answer that switches plugin.discovery back to hybrid_warn instead of adding the manifest misses m3, because the question keeps service_load.

must.text: Leaves topics that have a KafkaTopic resource out of the job's partition and configuration changes, because the Topic Operator reverts any change made to them outside the KafkaTopic; their retention has to change in the KafkaTopic's spec (the data-platform repository), for example by reporting the difference to that team.

Takes the Kafka topic name of each KafkaTopic from spec.topicName (or status.topicName) and falls back to metadata.name only when it is absent, because a name like cust-ACME_EU-events is not a valid Kubernetes resource name and can only be given in spec.topicName.

Changes retention.ms without resetting the topic's other overrides by using incremental_alter_configs with a ConfigEntry for retention.ms and AlterConfigOpType.SET, because alter_configs reverts every configuration it is not given to its default, which is what wiped cust-4711-events.

Only adds partitions (create_partitions with NewPartitions and the new total) when the topic has fewer than wanted and never asks for fewer, because Kafka cannot reduce the number of partitions of a topic.

Restores the overrides lost on cust-4711-events (cleanup.policy=compact,delete and min.insync.replicas=2) once, for example with kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config or an incremental SET; fixing the job does not bring them back.

Changes retention.ms without resetting the topic's other overrides by reading the topic's current overrides with describe_configs and passing all of them, with the new retention.ms, to alter_configs, because alter_configs reverts every configuration it is not given to its default.

must_not.text: Recommends deleting the data-platform team's KafkaTopic resources (or disabling the Topic Operator) so that the job can manage those topics again.
must_not.condition: only if recommended; annotating a KafkaTopic with strimzi.io/managed: "false" in agreement with its owners, which keeps the Kafka topic, does not count
must_not.near_miss: Annotating a KafkaTopic with strimzi.io/managed="false" stops the Topic Operator from reconciling it and keeps the Kafka topic.

must_not.text: States that in Strimzi 1.3.1 a change made directly in Kafka to a topic that has a KafkaTopic is kept or written back into the KafkaTopic resource.
must_not.condition: only if stated as the behaviour of Strimzi 1.3.1
must_not.near_miss: Configuration changes go one way, from the KafkaTopic resource to the Kafka topic; direct changes are reverted.

must_not.text: Claims that the Topic Operator deletes, reverts or takes over topics that have no KafkaTopic resource, so that the job's own topics need KafkaTopic resources to keep their settings.
must_not.condition: only if stated; recommending KafkaTopic resources for other reasons, such as keeping all topics in Git, does not count
must_not.near_miss: The Topic Operator does not interfere with topics that have no KafkaTopic resource.

correct_alternative:
Read the managed names from the KafkaTopic status, which carries the real Kafka name (cust-ACME_EU-events cannot be a Kubernetes metadata.name):

owned = {i["status"]["topicName"] for i in topics_json["items"] if i.get("status", {}).get("topicName")}

In the loop, `continue` for any name in owned and log it for the data-platform team: their KafkaTopic is the source of truth, and the Topic Operator puts back whatever the job changes. For the job's own topics:

want = ConfigResource("topic", name)
want.add_incremental_config(ConfigEntry("retention.ms", str(c.retention_ms), incremental_operation=AlterConfigOpType.SET))
admin.incremental_alter_configs([want])[want].result(timeout=30)
cur = len(md.topics[name].partitions)
if cur < c.partitions:
    admin.create_partitions([NewPartitions(name, c.partitions)])[name].result(timeout=30)
elif cur > c.partitions:
    log.warning("%s has %d partitions; Kafka cannot shrink it", name, cur)

The deprecated alter_configs sends the full configuration and resets everything not in the request, which is why cust-4711-events lost its overrides. Put them back with the same incremental call, two SET entries: cleanup.policy compact,delete and min.insync.replicas 2.
generic: Use the confluent-kafka AdminClient to keep topics in line with the database: list the topics, create the missing ones with the right partitions and replication factor, and update the retention of the existing ones. Make the job idempotent, log every change, handle errors and retries, and run it in a staging cluster first. Consider keeping topic definitions in version control.
note: m3 and m6 are an any_of group (incremental SET, or the read-all-then-alter workaround the client documents for alter_configs); both are not_indexed: the reset behaviour of alter_configs is stated only in the confluent-kafka 2.16.1 sources, and the indexed Kafka upgrade notes (upgrade.md:293) only call alterConfigs deprecated. must.text: Rejects NFS for broker data: Strimzi strongly recommends block storage, and file-system storage such as NFS is not guaranteed to work as primary broker storage.

Says that with local volumes a broker is tied to its worker: if the worker dies, the broker pod cannot be scheduled elsewhere and stays down until that worker is back.
Enables rack awareness with spec.kafka.rack.topologyKey set to a node label that holds the rack (r1, r2, r3), so that the replicas of each partition are placed in different racks.

Spreads brokers and controllers evenly over the racks with topologySpreadConstraints on the rack label in the KafkaNodePools (maxSkew 1), because rack awareness does not distribute the pods by itself.
Uses one KafkaNodePool per rack with node affinity to that rack's workers (two brokers and one controller per rack), because rack awareness does not distribute the pods by itself.

Checks the capacity: 100 MB/s x 172,800 s is about 17.3 TB per copy, about 52 TB with replication factor 3, about 8.6 TB per broker, roughly 56 % of the 15.36 TB raw on a broker's worker, so local NVMe fits with headroom; Ceph at size 3 would need about 156 TB raw for the same data, far more than the 40 TB free.

must_not.text: Says local volumes are provisioned dynamically by their StorageClass, so no PVs need to be created beforehand.
must_not.condition: only if stated or relied on in the design
must_not.near_miss: The StorageClass for local volumes provisions nothing; it only delays binding until the pod is scheduled.

must_not.condition: only if recommended for planned maintenance or for a worker that will come back; recommending it as a last resort after a worker or disk is lost for good does not count

reference:
Storage: not NFS. Strimzi strongly recommends block storage; NFS is not guaranteed to work for broker data. Use the workers' NVMe as local persistent volumes: statically created PVs, one per disk, each with nodeAffinity to its worker (local volumes have no dynamic provisioning), behind a StorageClass with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer so that binding waits until the pod is scheduled.
Capacity (decimal TB): 100 MB/s x 172,800 s = 17.3 TB per copy, x 3 = 51.8 TB, 8.6 TB per broker, 56 % of the 15.36 TB raw per worker: it fits, with room for peaks and imbalance. On Ceph at size 3 the same data needs about 156 TB raw against 40 TB free.
Placement: label the workers with their rack and set spec.kafka.rack.topologyKey to that label, so each partition's replicas land in three racks. Rack awareness does not spread pods, so add topologySpreadConstraints (maxSkew 1) on the rack label to the broker and controller KafkaNodePools: two brokers and one controller per rack.
Failures: a broker is tied to its worker. If the worker dies, the pod cannot start elsewhere; the broker stays down and its partitions run on two replicas until the worker is back. Patching likewise: drain, patch, uncordon, and wait until the broker is back in the ISR before the next worker. Only if a worker or disk is lost for good, replace the broker with strimzi.io/delete-pod-and-pvc after preparing a new PV; that deletes its data, and Kafka re-replicates from the other racks.
correct_alternative: Neither offer suits Kafka. NFS is file storage, which Strimzi does not guarantee for brokers, and Ceph RBD at size 3 triples Kafka's own three copies: 48 h x 100 MB/s x 3 is about 52 TB of log, about 156 TB raw on Ceph, and only 40 TB are free. Put the data on the NVMe in the workers instead, as local PVs created ahead of time (four per broker worker, each pinned with nodeAffinity; no dynamic provisioning for local volumes) and a no-provisioner StorageClass with WaitForFirstConsumer. Each broker then holds about 8.6 TB of 15.36 TB raw. Make one KafkaNodePool per rack, each with node affinity to its rack's workers: two brokers and one controller per rack. Set rack.topologyKey to the rack label so Kafka spreads replicas over the racks. Expect a broker to stay down while its worker is down, since its volumes cannot follow it; keep the delete-pod-and-pvc annotation for a worker that is gone for good, as it wipes that broker's data.
generic: For Kafka on Kubernetes, use fast persistent storage and spread brokers across failure domains. Plan for enough disk capacity with headroom for growth, monitor disk usage, and set retention appropriately. Use pod anti-affinity so brokers do not share nodes, and drain nodes carefully during maintenance so that the cluster stays available.
note: m6 is arithmetic and not_indexed. Not a point but true: replicated storage is not required (con-considerations-for-data-storage.adoc:49). The delete-pod-and-pvc page still names broker pods <cluster>-kafka-<index>, the pre-node-pool naming. Second review: m3 is now the answer to 'what happens when a worker dies' (volumes.md:662-666); the StorageClass with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer (storage-classes.md:478-484) stays in both answers but is not a point, because the item is at six units. The correct alternative takes m5b and computes the same capacity.

Run both methods side by side and move applications one at a time.
Listener: leave scram (9093) unchanged and add a second internal listener, for example oauth on 9095 with tls: true and authentication type custom: sasl: true and listenerConfig with sasl.enabled.mechanisms: OAUTHBEARER, oauthbearer.sasl.server.callback.handler.class: io.strimzi.kafka.oauth.server.JaasServerOauthValidatorCallbackHandler and an OAuthBearerLoginModule JAAS configuration (oauth.valid.issuer.uri, oauth.jwks.endpoint.uri, oauth.username.claim, truststore for Keycloak). The draft's type oauth is deprecated, and the v1 schema of Strimzi 1.3.1 accepts only tls, scram-sha-512 and custom. Add principal.builder.class: io.strimzi.kafka.oauth.server.OAuthKafkaPrincipalBuilder to spec.kafka.config; the claim you choose becomes the principal name your ACLs must use.
Keycloak load: validate JWTs locally with the JWKS endpoint (cached keys). Introspection calls Keycloak for every new connection, and 120 applications with 5 to 50 connections each reconnect often enough to matter.
Tokens: set connections.max.reauth.ms on the oauth listener (for example 300000) so that connections re-authenticate with fresh tokens, and have applications use client credentials with io.strimzi.kafka.oauth.client.JaasClientOauthLoginCallbackHandler, which refreshes tokens; no long-lived manual tokens.
Authorization: keep simple during the migration. For each migrated application create a KafkaUser without authentication, named after its OAuth principal and carrying the same ACLs; the User Operator writes them in the SASL username format. Switch to authorization type custom with KeycloakAuthorizer only after the last SCRAM application has moved; doing it earlier needs strimzi.authorization.delegate.to.kafka.acl: "true", because authorization applies to all listeners, and supportsAdminApi: true so that the User Operator keeps managing the KafkaUser ACLs. Remove the scram listener and the SCRAM KafkaUsers last.
correct_alternative: Split the draft in two and stretch it over the six months. Phase 1: add an OAuth listener next to scram, using authentication type custom with OAUTHBEARER and JaasServerOauthValidatorCallbackHandler (type oauth is deprecated and not in the 1.3.1 v1 schema), principal.builder.class set to OAuthKafkaPrincipalBuilder, local token validation against Keycloak's JWKS endpoint so brokers do not call Keycloak per connection as introspection would, and connections.max.reauth.ms so long-lived connections re-authenticate before the 5-minute tokens run out; clients use the client-credentials flow with the Strimzi callback handler, which renews tokens. Phase 2, in the same change as the listener: authorization type custom with KeycloakAuthorizer, supportsAdminApi: true (so the User Operator keeps managing the KafkaUser ACLs) and strimzi.authorization.delegate.to.kafka.acl: "true". Authorization is cluster-wide, so without delegation every SCRAM application, whose rights are Kafka ACLs, would be denied. Applications then get Keycloak policies as they move. When the last one has moved, drop the scram listener and, if wanted, the delegation.
generic: Migrating to OAuth centralises identity management. Plan the migration carefully, test it in staging first and communicate with the application teams. Configure the Kafka listener for OAuth, register the clients in Keycloak and update the client configurations. Monitor authentication errors and Keycloak load during the rollout, and keep a rollback plan.
note: Sources disagree: con-oauth-migration.adoc:7 says the oauth and keycloak types are deprecated and 'will be removed', but the v1 schema in 1.3.1 already lists only tls, scram-sha-512 and custom for listeners (appendix_crds.adoc:159; 040-Crd-kafka.yaml:110-116) and simple and custom for authorization (040-Crd-kafka.yaml:434-437). The docs' JWKS example sets connections.max.reauth.ms: 3600, which is milliseconds (3.6 s); the reference uses 300000. con-oauth-authz-config.adoc:15 says Keycloak Authorization Services is the only supported authorization mechanism for OAuth-based permissions; simple ACLs on OAuth principals (m6a) rest on the KafkaUser schema (appendix_crds.adoc:2872). must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: this is the default high-availability task assignment working as designed, not a fault: a stateful task moves to a new pod only after a warmup replica there has restored its state to within acceptable.recovery.lag of the changelog end; until then the old pod keeps the task active, which is why the old pods stay busy.
Explains the pace: active tasks move to the new instances at most at max.warmup.replicas (default 2) per probing.rebalance.interval.ms (default 10 minutes), so about 2 tasks per 10 minutes.
To balance faster next time, raises max.warmup.replicas so that more tasks warm up at once.
To balance faster next time, lowers probing.rebalance.interval.ms so that warmups that have caught up are promoted to active tasks sooner.

Checks it without changing anything by re-running the member listing (kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group fraud-features --members, optionally with --verbose to see the assigned partitions) every few minutes and watching the new members gain partitions a couple at a time.

must_not.text: Recommends deleting the new pods' PVCs or state directories, or running the application reset tool, to make the new pods take over their tasks.
must_not.condition: only if recommended as a step; saying not to do it, or describing what the reset tool would do, does not count
must_not.near_miss: Leave the state in place: the new pods are restoring it from the changelogs, and wiping it only starts the restore again.

must_not.text: Explains the idle new pods by there being more instances (or stream threads) than partitions.
must_not.condition: only as the explanation for this case; noting in general that partitions bound the parallelism does not count
must_not.near_miss: Partitions bound the parallelism, but 64 partitions over 8 single-thread pods allows 8 tasks per pod.

reference:
Nothing is broken. Kafka Streams' default high-availability assignment does not hand a stateful task to a new instance until that instance has a caught-up copy of its state. After the scale-out it put warmup replicas on the new pods; they restore from the changelogs (the steady reads you see), and a task moves only when its warmup is within acceptable.recovery.lag (10,000 records by default) of the changelog end. Until then the old pod keeps the task active, so the old pods stay hot.

The pace comes from two defaults: max.warmup.replicas=2 warmups at a time, and warmups are promoted only at probing rebalances every probing.rebalance.interval.ms=10 minutes. That is about 2 tasks per 10 minutes. To reach 8 tasks per pod, 32 of the 64 tasks must move, so at least about 160 minutes; 12 moved in the first hour, which matches your listing.

To check without changing anything, run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group fraud-features --members --verbose every few minutes: the CURRENT-ASSIGNMENT column shows partitions arriving on the new members a couple at a time.

Do not delete the PVCs or run the reset tool: the restore would start over, and the reset tool reprocesses from scratch. It is not a partition limit either: 64 partitions allow 8 per pod.

Next time, raise max.warmup.replicas (for example to 8) so more tasks warm up in parallel, at the cost of more changelog traffic, or lower probing.rebalance.interval.ms (minimum 1 minute).
correct_alternative:
This is warmup-based task movement, not a bug. A stateful task is only given to a new pod once that pod's warmup copy of the store is within acceptable.recovery.lag of the changelog; meanwhile the old pod keeps processing it. Warmups are promoted at probing rebalances, every probing.rebalance.interval.ms (10 minutes by default), with at most max.warmup.replicas (2) at a time: about 2 tasks per 10 minutes, so the 32 moves need roughly 2 hours 40 minutes in total. Your 12 moves after an hour fit.

Watch it read-only: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group fraud-features --members --verbose, repeated every few minutes, lists the partitions per member.

Keep the PVCs; wiping them restarts the restore. For future scale-outs, set probing.rebalance.interval.ms to 1 or 2 minutes (1 minute is the minimum) so caught-up warmups are swapped in sooner.
generic: Kafka Streams rebalances tasks when new instances join the group. Check the new pods' logs for errors and make sure they can reach the brokers. Restoring large state stores can take time, so monitor the consumer group lag and the pods' resources. If the problem persists, restart the new pods or give them more CPU and memory, and check that the topic has enough partitions for eight instances.
note: Two pages answer it (running-app.md and config-streams.md / streams_config.html). The 160-minute figure assumes each warmup finishes within one probing interval; with 6 GB per task it may take longer, so a range is acceptable. Setting acceptable.recovery.lag to Long.MAX_VALUE is documented (config-streams.md) as a way to get an immediate balanced assignment at the cost of blocking processing while restoring; it is neither required nor penalised. Switching to group.protocol=streams is not required (that protocol has no warmup tasks, streams-rebalance-protocol.md). Second review: m2 reduced to the documented rate (the 160-minute total is in the reference); the any_of group m3/m4 is weight 2 because the question asks for it; the evidence follows the 4.3 tool layout (GROUP column).

must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: in sourceConnector.config the producer.* keys configure only the producer that writes the offset-syncs topic; the producer that sends the replicated records to the target is configured with producer.override.*, so the batch, linger and compression change never reached it.
Moves the settings to producer.override.batch.size, producer.override.linger.ms and producer.override.compression.type in sourceConnector.config.
Recommends running MirrorMaker 2 next to the target (us) cluster, consuming from the remote eu cluster and producing locally, because producers suffer more than consumers from a high-latency link.

Sets producer.batch.size, producer.linger.ms and producer.compression.type in spec.target.config instead, the Kafka Connect worker configuration of the KafkaMirrorMaker2, where the producer. prefix configures the producers of all source tasks.

must_not.text: Recommends raising producer.batch.size or producer.linger.ms further, or adding more producer.* (not producer.override.*) keys to sourceConnector.config, as the fix for throughput.
must_not.condition: only with the plain producer. prefix in sourceConnector.config; the same values under producer.override. in sourceConnector.config, or as producer.* worker settings in spec.target.config, do not count
must_not.near_miss: Set producer.override.batch.size, producer.override.linger.ms and producer.override.compression.type.

must_not.text: Recommends keeping (or moving) the MirrorMaker 2 deployment next to the source cluster as the better placement for this link.
must_not.condition: only as a recommendation; describing the current placement does not count
must_not.near_miss: Run MirrorMaker 2 next to the target: consume from remote, produce to local.

reference:
The tuning never reached the producer that matters. In a KafkaMirrorMaker2 sourceConnector, producer.* keys configure only the producer that writes the offset-syncs topic. The producer that sends the replicated records to the target cluster takes its settings from producer.override.*. So the replication producer still runs with default batching and no compression, which is why not even the bytes on the link changed; with about 85 ms per round trip, small uncompressed batches cap the throughput.

Change the connector config to:

sourceConnector:
  tasksMax: 12
  config:
    producer.override.batch.size: 524288
    producer.override.linger.ms: 50
    producer.override.compression.type: zstd

Second, move MirrorMaker 2 next to the us cluster. The geo-replication guidance is consume from remote, produce to local: producers suffer more from high-latency links than consumers, and the consumer side can fetch large batches over the WAN.

While you are at it, rule out a quota: a flat ceiling around 32 MB/s is also what a produce byte-rate quota on the MirrorMaker 2 user looks like. Check the throttle-time attribute of kafka.server:type=Produce,user=<mm2 user>,client-id=... on the us brokers; it should be 0.

After the change, compare byte-rate and record-age-ms of kafka.connect.mirror:type=MirrorSourceConnector again during the evening peak.
correct_alternative: The producer.batch.size, producer.linger.ms and producer.compression.type lines in sourceConnector.config are valid keys, but in the source connector the producer. prefix belongs to the small producer that writes offset syncs; the replicated records are sent by the Kafka Connect worker's producer, which is why nothing changed, not even the link bytes. Configure that producer at the worker level instead: remove the three lines from sourceConnector.config and put producer.batch.size: 524288, producer.linger.ms: 50 and producer.compression.type: zstd under spec.target.config, the Connect worker configuration of the KafkaMirrorMaker2, where producer.-prefixed settings apply to the producers of all source tasks. Then relocate MirrorMaker 2 to the us side, so the WAN hop is on the consumer side; Kafka's guidance is to place MirrorMaker close to the target cluster because producers handle high latency worse than consumers.
generic: Cross-region replication is limited by latency and bandwidth. Increase tasksMax so that more tasks replicate in parallel, tune batch size, linger and compression, check the network bandwidth between the regions and the broker load on both sides, and watch the MirrorMaker 2 metrics such as record age and replication latency to see whether the changes help.
note: One of the easier items: two pages (the Strimzi producers-and-consumers page and the Kafka geo-replication page) answer it. Raising tasksMax is not penalised (48 partitions allow it) but does not fix the cause. Second review: the replication producer can be reached in two documented ways, producer.override.* in sourceConnector.config (m2) or producer.* worker settings in spec.target.config (m5), an any_of group; the correct_alternative takes m5. The quota check (old m4) was dropped as a must point; it stays in the reference and is not penalised. m3 (MirrorMaker 2 next to the target) is the same fact as p2-18 m1, here at weight 1 in a different family.

Gets the current sync unstuck by terminating the running sync operation (Terminate in the UI's sync panel, or argocd app terminate-op kafka-prod-config).

Cleans up the hook Job with the default BeforeHookCreation policy (implicit, or set with argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy) and the fixed metadata.name, so that Argo CD deletes the previous Job just before creating the next one.
Cleans up the hook Job with argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded, so that Argo CD deletes the Job after the sync succeeds (this also works with generateName).

Explains the 41 change records: hooks run on every sync (including self-heal syncs, manual syncs and syncs of unrelated changes), not only when the Kafka configuration changed, so each of those syncs announced a change.

Makes the announcement safe to run more than once, so that a repeated sync of the same Git revision does not open another change record (for example the event carries the revision as its key and the hook or the change-calendar consumer skips a revision already announced).

Removes ttlSecondsAfterFinished from the hook Job.

must_not.condition: only as the recommended fix for the hook Job; a TTL on Jobs that are not Argo CD hooks does not count
must_not.near_miss: Remove ttlSecondsAfterFinished from the hook and let the hook-delete-policy clean up.

must_not.text: Recommends going back to generateName and relying on BeforeHookCreation (the default) to delete the old Jobs.
must_not.condition: only if BeforeHookCreation is named as the cleanup for generateName Jobs; generateName with HookSucceeded does not count

reference:
The sync is waiting for a Job that Kubernetes has already deleted. Argo CD decides whether the PostSync phase worked by reading the hook Job. With ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 0 the TTL-after-finished controller deletes the Job as soon as it completes, before Argo CD has read it, so the operation waits for a hook that no longer exists and the app stays Progressing. The Argo CD docs say to avoid ttlSecondsAfterFinished on hook Jobs and to clean up with the hook-delete-policy instead.

Now: terminate the running operation (Terminate in the sync panel, or argocd app terminate-op kafka-prod-config), fix the manifest and sync again. Terminating does not undo what the hook did: this sync's event was already sent.

The hook: remove ttlSecondsAfterFinished. With the fixed metadata.name you can rely on the default BeforeHookCreation policy: Argo CD deletes the previous Job just before creating the next one, so only the last run is kept. That policy is meant for a fixed name, which is why the generateName Jobs piled up.

The 41 change records: hooks run on every sync, not only when something they care about changed. With selfHeal on, every self-heal, every manual sync and every sync of an unrelated change runs the PostSync Job again. Make the announcement safe to run twice: put the Git revision into the event as the record key, and let the hook or the change-calendar consumer skip a revision that was already announced.
correct_alternative: Kubernetes' TTL controller removes the finished Job at once (ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 0), but Argo CD has to read that Job to finish the PostSync phase, so it waits for a hook that is gone; the Argo CD documentation warns against TTLs on hook Jobs. Unblock the app with argocd app terminate-op kafka-prod-config (or Terminate in the UI) and sync again. For cleanup, drop the TTL and annotate the Job with argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded: Argo CD deletes it after a successful sync, and this works with generateName as well, while failed runs stay for inspection. The extra change records come from hooks running on every sync, including self-heal syncs and syncs of unrelated changes. Instead of announcing from a hook, remove the Job and let Argo CD Notifications send the change event to the change-calendar service with an on-deployed trigger that has oncePer: app.status.sync.revision, so there is one notification per Git revision.
generic: Argo CD hooks run Jobs before or after a sync. If a sync is stuck, check the application controller logs and the Job's pods, make sure the Job exits successfully, and refresh or hard-refresh the application. You can also raise the sync timeout or add retries to the sync policy. For the change records, ask the change-calendar team to review their integration.
note: Argo CD-centred debugging item; two Argo CD pages answer most of it (sync-waves.md, sections 'Hook lifecycle and cleanup' and 'Things to keep in mind', and faq.md for terminating), with ttlafterfinished.md for the Kubernetes side. Second review: the TTL removal is its own point m8 (weight 2); the cleanup-policy group m3/m4 is weight 1; m6 and m7 accept any once-per-revision mechanism.

Sets the same offset-syncs.topic.location: target in checkpointConnector.config, because the checkpoint connector reads the offset-syncs topic and the property must have the same value in both connectors.

Makes sure the MirrorMaker 2 user on analytics (its KafkaUser ACLs) can read and write the offset-syncs topic there, since the connectors still need read and write access to that topic where it is located.
Verifies the fix by checking that retail.checkpoints.internal on analytics starts receiving checkpoint records.

must_not.condition: only if the answer's configuration or instructions set it in one connector and not the other
must_not.near_miss: Set offset-syncs.topic.location: target in both sourceConnector.config and checkpointConnector.config.

The missing piece is the offset-syncs topic. The MirrorSourceConnector records how source offsets map to target offsets in an internal topic, mm2-offset-syncs.analytics.internal, and by default it creates and writes that topic in the source cluster, retail. Your ACLs on retail are read-only, so the creates and writes are denied. The checkpoint connector builds its checkpoints from those offset syncs, so retail.checkpoints.internal stays empty and no fulfil-* offsets reach analytics.

Move the topic to the target. In the KafkaMirrorMaker2:

sourceConnector:

The plan needs three changes.

1. exactly_once is gone. EOS version 1 is no longer supported since 4.0; 4.3.2 accepts only at_least_once and exactly_once_v2. Switch to exactly_once_v2 first, as its own rolling bounce while still on 3.2.3 (the upgrade guide's path for 3.0+ applications). Only then upgrade the version.

3. Capture service: isolation.level=read_committed. The default read_uncommitted also returns records of aborted transactions, i.e. duplicates.

Caveat: exactly-once ends at Kafka. The capture call is an external side effect; if the service crashes after the call and before its offset commit, the record is read again and captured again. reference:
Keep the single KafkaMirrorMaker2 next to the central cluster, but drop IdentityReplicationPolicy. With the default DefaultReplicationPolicy each region lands in its own remote topic: eu.orders, us.orders and ap.orders. That prefix is what keeps records from different clusters out of the same topic-partition; IdentityReplicationPolicy is meant for one-way replication from one source, such as a migration or failover, not for merging three sources into one orders topic.

For the analytics jobs, subscribe to the three topics, by list or by a pattern such as (eu|us|ap)\.orders. Order is kept per partition within each region, not across regions.

Protect the central cluster from catch-up bursts: after a two-hour outage, eu alone has up to 48 MB/s x 7,200 s = about 345 GB to replay. Give the MirrorMaker 2 KafkaUser a spec.quotas.producerByteRate so the replay cannot starve other clients.

Sizing at peak: 48 + 30 + 12 = 90 MB/s in; with RF 3 that is 270 MB/s of disk writes, about 45 MB/s per broker, plus the matching replica fetch traffic. Retention: 90 MB/s x 259,200 s = about 23 TB per copy, about 70 TB with RF 3, about 11.7 TB per broker if the peak lasted all day; the real figure follows the average rate.

Missing numbers: average rates per region, the regional retention versus the longest outage (MirrorMaker 2 can only catch up on data still retained), and the inter-region bandwidth available for catching up.
correct_alternative: Use the default naming, not identity: under DefaultReplicationPolicy the topics arrive as eu.orders, us.orders and ap.orders, so MirrorMaker 2 never writes two regions into the same topic-partition; Strimzi describes IdentityReplicationPolicy for unidirectional replication, migration or failover. To keep one input for the analytics jobs, run a small Kafka Streams job in the central cluster that merges the three remote topics into orders-all; the merged stream keeps order within each input but has none across regions. Put a producerByteRate quota on MirrorMaker 2's KafkaUser in the central cluster so the backlog after a link outage is replayed at a bounded rate. Size for 90 MB/s at peak (270 MB/s of writes with RF 3, ~45 MB/s per broker) and up to ~23 TB per copy, ~70 TB with RF 3, for 3 days. Still needed: average rates, regional retention versus outage length, and inter-region bandwidth.
generic: MirrorMaker 2 can replicate topics from several clusters into a central cluster. Configure one mirror per source cluster, choose a replication policy that fits your naming needs, monitor replication lag, and make sure the central cluster has enough brokers, disk and network capacity for the combined traffic and retention.
